> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

text.text: Supernatural concepts are often thought to gain cultural attraction by violating intuitive expectations in limited ways, but many theological doctrines also involve logical contradictions or impossibilities.
It remains unclear how such formal violations influence people's evaluations of religious propositions.

In the present study, 96 Japanese adults rated 20 fictional theological propositions on dimensions related to perceived value, including importance, profundity, interestingness, sacredness, and shareability, and on impossibility and logical contradiction.
A composite positiveevaluation score was derived from items rating perceived value.

A repeated-measures ANOVA showed that positive evaluation differed across categories: logically contradictory propositions were rated higher than tautological propositions, and counterintuitive propositions were rated higher than empirical propositions.

Further linear mixed-effects models, with propositions as random effects, showed that higher impossibility and logical contradiction, combined as incomprehensibility, predicted higher positive evaluations.
These findings suggest that impossible and contradictory theological content can be positively evaluated.

The Minimally Counterintuitive (MCI) theory proposes that supernatural concepts that violate intuitive expectations in limited ways are more memorable and culturally transmissible than concepts that are either entirely ordinary or overwhelmingly bizarre (Norenzayan et al., 2006).
text.formatted: The Minimally Counterintuitive (MCI) theory proposes that supernatural concepts that violate intuitive expectations in limited ways are more memorable and culturally transmissible than concepts that are either entirely ordinary or overwhelmingly bizarre <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Norenzayan et al., 2006)</ref>.

text.text: Empirical studies support this claim through recall experiments (Barrett & Nyhof, 2001; Boyer & Ramble, 2001) and analyses of folkloric materials (Barrett et al., 2009; Nakawake et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Empirical studies support this claim through recall experiments <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Barrett & Nyhof, 2001;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">Boyer & Ramble, 2001)</ref> and analyses of folkloric materials <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Barrett et al., 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Nakawake et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: In these studies, counterintuitiveness is typically defined as violations of ontological expectations (e.g., a ghost that passes through walls, thereby violating folk physics).

However, supernatural concepts could also violate more abstract cognitive principles. Atran and Norenzayan (2004) argue that religious ideas may violate universal expectations about the everyday structure of the world, and that such violations can strengthen religious belief and tradition (Atran, 2016).
text.formatted: However, supernatural concepts could also violate more abstract cognitive principles. <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">Atran and Norenzayan (2004)</ref> argue that religious ideas may violate universal expectations about the everyday structure of the world, and that such violations can strengthen religious belief and tradition <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Atran, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Some core theological doctrines involve not merely ontological violations but logical contradictions or modal impossibilities (in modal logic, modality refers to the concept of necessity/possibility).
For example, the Trinity or the Hypostatic Union (the claim that Jesus is fully divine and fully human).
Similar paradoxical formulations appear across traditions.

These cases raise the question of whether violations of logic and modality function similarly to minimally counterintuitive concepts, or whether they instead constitute maximally counterintuitive content that hinders cultural transmission.
The present study asks whether logical contradiction and impossibility enhance the perceived value of fictional theological propositions.
If such features increase perceived value, this would suggest that the MCI framework may extend beyond ontological violations to violations of more formal and abstract cognitive principles.
This question also connects to a broader debate about the relationship between religion and science.
In scientific reasoning, logical contradiction is treated as error.

From a theory that entails both a proposition and its negation (both P and not P), the principle of explosion allows you to logically conclude anything (P ∧ ¬P ⊢ Q, Q being any proposition), including empirically false statements.
For example, from the Hypostatic Union (Jesus is human and Jesus is not human), you can conclude any propositions, like "there is no physical reality".
Thus, theories with contradiction are instantly falsified (Popper, 2002).
text.formatted: Thus, theories with contradiction are instantly falsified <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Popper, 2002)</ref>.

text.text: From this perspective, religious doctrines that assert contradictions or logical impossibilities may appear epistemically defective.
Hence, rationalist critiques of religion deem religion to be of no value.
Such stance has been championed by Richard Dawkins, who once called religion "a betrayal of the intellect" (Cambridge Union, 2013).
text.formatted: Such stance has been championed by Richard Dawkins, who once called religion "a betrayal of the intellect" <ref type="bibr">(Cambridge Union, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: By contrast, Gould's (1997) Non-Overlapping Magisteria (NOMA) thesis proposes that science and religion operate in distinct domains: science addresses facts, whereas religion concerns meaning and value.
text.formatted: By contrast, <ref type="bibr">Gould's (1997)</ref> Non-Overlapping Magisteria (NOMA) thesis proposes that science and religion operate in distinct domains: science addresses facts, whereas religion concerns meaning and value.

text.text: If so, contradiction and impossibility in religious contexts may not be treated by scientific standards.
Whether individuals actually evaluate such unscientific features as defects or not remains an empirical question.
We hypothesized that propositions involving logical contradiction or impossibility would receive higher positive evaluations than propositions without such violations.
Participants were recruited via Lancers, a Japanese online crowdsourcing platform.
Of 112 responses, 16 were excluded (15 unfinished, 1 missing age), yielding a final sample of N = 96 (74 men, 22 women; M age = 45.20, SD = 8.22, range = 25-65).
This sample size was decided heuristically based on preceding experiments about MCI theory (e.g., "Boyer and Ramble, 2001", employed 18-81 participants per experiment).
Moreover, each participant rated 20 propositions, yielding a larger number of observations for the main analysis.
The majority reported no religious affiliation (n = 66), with others identifying primarily as Buddhist (n = 23) or another tradition (n = 7).
The study was approved by the Knowledge Science Ethics Council of Japan Advanced Institute of Science and Technology (Approval No.
Participants received 150 yen upon completion.
(2)Materials Twenty fictional theological propositions were constructed by adapting themes from Christianity, Judaism, Islam, and Buddhism (see Supplementary 1).

We coined a fictional and meaningless deity name, "God Ijasuto," (e.g., from "Jesus is both father and son", we made "God Ijasuto was born from its mother, yet simultaneously gave birth to that mother").
To prevent name-specific associations from influencing participants' evaluations and see purely the effect of formal variations of propositions, we used the same deity's name across twenty sentences.

When we prepared propositions, we designed them to fit into five categories (four items per category): Logically Contradictory (LC), Unimaginable (UI), Counterintuitive (CI), Empirical (EM), and Tautological (TT).
For Tautological, we prepared propositions whose contents were "X is X".
For Logically Contradictory, we prepared propositions whose contents are "X is A and not A".
Items in these two categories are thematically matched; for example, "Because God Ijasuto embodies justice, Ijasuto is a being of justice (TT)" and "God Ijasuto is good, yet commits evil (LC)".

Similarly, Counterintuitive and Empirical are to be reversed categories, thus we also paired propositions thematically ("God Ijasuto split a mountain"(CI) and "God Ijasuto walked in the mountains"(EM)).
For CI, items here are designed to violate ontological categories following Barrett's coding (Barrett, 2008).

text.text: Items in EM can be understood as ordinary text which will not violate ontological categories.
For UI, items here do not have thematic correspondence to items in other categories.
Unlike other categories, we did not have specific formal criteria for preparing items here.

This is because we directly adopted semantic contents from monotheistic traditions (Islam, Christian, Kabbala) that we found hardly imaginable (e.g., "God Ijasuto was originally the Word, yet now Ijasuto dies as a human being" was adopted from Christian text).
(3)Procedure The online survey consisted of two phases, in which participants evaluated the same set of propositions.

In Phase 1, participants were presented with twenty propositions framed as religious claims about a fictional deity ("God Ijasuto") in random order and rated each proposition (rather than the concept of God Ijasuto) on seven value-related dimensions (importance, profundity, banality, interestingness, sacredness, shareability, difficulty of abandoning) using 7-point Likert scales (1=strongly disagree,7=strongly agree.
See supplementary for the actual question sentence).
Throughout Phase 1, we used the same deity's name "God Ijasuto".
This was to prevent name-specific associations from affecting participants' evaluations of propositions.
Also, the order of propositions was random and counterbalanced, so that the effect of chronological order is partially canceled.

In Phase 2, the same propositions were reframed as neutral, non-religious statements by replacing the deity's name "God Ijasuto" with the label "A," and the same propositions were presented in random order.

Participants were asked to read them as non-religious, ordinary texts, and rated four formal properties of each proposition: impossibility, logical contradiction, self-evidence, and imaginability (7-point scales).

We replaced the subject with a neutral label because explicit reasoning about God tends to invoke a theologically correct concept of an omnipotent being unconstrained by ordinary limits (Barrett & Keil, 1996), and context alters how counterintuitive content is processed (Upal et al., 2007).

text.text: Thus, "God Ijasuto exists, yet does not exist" might seem less contradictory than "A exists, yet does not exist" simply because "God is beyond our understanding and can do anything."
Measuring the formal properties in a separate phase also reduced the risk that value and formal judgments would influence each other.
Lastly, participants completed demographic questions (age, gender, religious affiliation, region).
(4)Analysis For preparing dependent variable, the seven Phase 1 evaluation items were submitted for exploratory factor analysis (see Results).
Five items were retained and averaged to form a composite positive evaluation score for each participant-proposition observation.
We carried out two analyses.
The first analysis compared the positive evaluation score across the five proposition categories (LC, UI, CI, EM, and TT).
For each participant, the scores for the four propositions in each category were averaged, and the five category means were compared with a one-way repeated-measures ANOVA.
Following the ANOVA, all ten pairwise comparisons among the five categories were tested with paired t-tests, with Holm adjustment across the ten comparisons.
Of these, we focused on two contrasts corresponding to the thematically matched categories: LC vs.
TT (logical contradiction) and CI vs.
EM (impossibility).
We predicted that LC propositions would be rated higher than TT propositions, and CI propositions higher than EM propositions.
The second analysis examined whether Phase 2 ratings predicted positive evaluations.
Proposition-participant-level predictors were Phase 2 ratings of impossibility and logical contradiction.
Self-evidence and imaginability were included as reverse-form manipulation checks and we did not intend to use them as predictors.
Thus, these items were not included in the second analysis.
We predicted that higher Phase 2 ratings of logical contradiction and impossibility predict higher Phase 1 positive evaluation scores.
The second analysis was conducted using linear mixed-effects models fitted with the lme4 package (Bates et al., 2015) and p values obtained via lmerTest package (Kuznetsova et al., 2017).

text.text: The present study examined whether impossibility and logical contradiction in fictional theological propositions predict positive evaluation.

Positive evaluation differed across the predefined proposition categories: logically contradictory propositions were rated higher than their matched tautological propositions, and counterintuitive propositions were rated higher than their matched empirical propositions.
Consistent with our hypothesis, impossibility and logical contradiction (combined, incomprehensibility) also predicted higher positive evaluation scores in a mixed-effects model.
We discuss two implications: (1) the scope of the MCI framework, (2) the cultural persistence of religion.
(1)Extending the MCI framework to formal violations Classical MCI research operationalizes counterintuitiveness as the violation of a small number of ontological expectations.
Our results suggest that violations of logic and modality do not diminish the appeal of theological content but rather enhance its perceived value.

Though we only tested the value judgements and not memorability, and the persistent use of the same deity's name in Phase 1 might have led participants to have built-up effect and risked the independence of each item, our result supports the possibility of extending the MCI framework beyond ontological violations.

(2)Implication for the cultural persistence of religion We consider that our findings have implications on the question of why religion survives scientific progress, and the relationship between science and religion.
The Dawkinsian rationalist critique predicts that contradictory and impossible propositions should be devalued, particularly by non-religious individuals.

Our result shows the opposite pattern: the majority of the participants were not associated with any religion, but still impossibility and logical contradiction predicted higher positive evaluation scores.
Positive evaluation of formally violating content was thus not confined to believers.

This pattern is more consistent with Gould's NOMA thesis: people appear not to apply the standards of scientific inference when evaluating theological propositions, regardless of their level of religious commitment.

Contradiction and impossibility functioned less as defects but rather boosted the appeal and importance of fictional religious propositions -consistent with the view that religious and scientific reasoning constitute distinct evaluative domains.

Our result, taken together with NOMA, is not only compatible with, but also corroborates some accounts about the mysterious and incomprehensible nature of religion. Sperber (2010) argued that the mysterious nature serves to boost the authority, significance and relevance of religion.

Atran (2016) noted that sacred values commit believers to sacrificial actions, and religious consensus over sacred values does not involve fact checking and reasoned argument, scientific inference in short, but results from rituals and emotional bonding.

text.text: Atran also argued that the incomprehensible nature of religion renders religion immune to scientific falsification.
Our study measured only perceived value, and thus cannot show whether logical and modal violations actually shield religious doctrines from scientific falsification, as Atran suggests.
Whether they do so remains an open question for future research, which could examine, for instance, how people respond to scientific criticism of contradictory versus non-contradictory doctrines.

Around the world, many people continue to adhere to various religions and systems of belief.
Some of these are long-established traditions, whereas others are newer religious movements.
They also include beliefs that may be regarded as superstitions, as well as religious beliefs and teachings that have largely disappeared.
A religion is generally not composed of a single teaching, but rather of multiple teachings.
Although these teachings are all considered important, they often differ in their relative importance and in the degree to which they are believed.
In the following section, you will read a series of teachings drawn from various religions and folk beliefs.
Please note that these teachings do not correspond to any real existing religion.
Rather, they were reconstructed by the researchers based on elements extracted from a wide variety of religious and folk traditions from different historical periods and cultures.
You will then be presented with a number of these teachings.
For each one, please indicate your own impression.
Please respond intuitively without spending too much time thinking about your answers.
For each teaching, indicate the extent to which you agree with the following statements using a 7-point scale ranging from 1 (Not at all) to 7 (Very much), with 4 (Neither) as the midpoint.
 Importance: How important and indispensable is this teaching to the religion?
 Profundity: To what extent does this teaching seem profound, deep, or difficult to fully comprehend?
 Ordinariness: To what extent does this teaching seem ordinary or commonplace?
 Interestingness: To what extent does this teaching seem interesting or engaging?
 Sacredness: To what extent does this teaching seem sacred or inviolable?
 Willingness to Share: To what extent would you want to tell other people about this teaching?
 Difficulty of Abandonment: How difficult would it be to persuade a believer in this teaching to abandon it?

text.text: The two factors were highly correlated (r = .753), suggesting that the two-factor structure does not represent meaningfully distinct constructs.
Given these considerations, we adopted the one-factor solution for constructing the composite dependent variable.
Items 3 (Banal) and 7 (Difficult to Abandon) showed weak loadings on the one-factor solution (≤ .37) and low corrected item-total correlations (r drop < .34; see Table S3).
